title: Standing at the Edge, with Roshi Joan Halifax

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for modern mutants interested in mindfulness, meditation, awakening, compassion, and much more. My name is Michael W. Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm very happy to be speaking with Roshi Joan Halifax. Roshi Joan Halifax, PhD, is a Buddhist teacher, Zen priest, anthropologist, and pioneer in the field of end-of-life care. She is founder, abbot, and head teacher of Upaya Institute and Zen Center in Santa Fe, New Mexico, a founding teacher of the Zen Peacemaker Order, and founder of the Prajna Mountain Buddhist Order. Her work and practice for more than four decades has focused on engaged Buddhism. Her books include The Fruitful Darkness, Being with Dying, and her new book, Standing at the Edge: Finding Freedom Where Fear and Courage Meet. And now, without further ado, I give you the episode that I call "Standing at the Edge."

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Roshi, I'm so glad to have you here on the Deconstructing Yourself podcast. Welcome.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Happy to be here, Michael. And also, it's wonderful to be here in the Bay Area.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Isn't it gorgeous?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It's not only gorgeous, it's far out.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: What are you noticing at the far out level of the Bay?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: So much cultural diversity. Yesterday I took a walk and ended up in the midst of Chinese New Year, and actually walked the street several times just milling in this huge crowd, listening to various dialects of Chinese being spoken, seeing all ages. The most amusing thing was — we talk about commodification of Buddhism in the West, but seeing the booth where a Buddhist monk is selling prayers…

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Interesting. Asia is no stranger to commodification of Buddhism.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Hardly. But it brought me actually a lot of joy to be in such a concentrated community of people of all ages who were non-Western, non-Anglo, and who were enjoying their own culture so much. And it felt safe — that was one of the things that I was appreciating. Sometimes there's an intolerance of difference in our society, and here there was a lot of consistency and a lot of fun.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's so beautiful. That community has been in San Francisco for maybe 150 years.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Yeah. Well, I think they built the Big Sur Highway.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Among many other things. And also they faced enormous discrimination. And somehow the Chinese character, which we're certainly aware of these days — culturally, socially, economically — has been a source of enormous strength and determination. Who knows what the outcome is going to be of China's relationship with the West. We can hope it is a positive one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Roshi, you have a new book out, or coming out, called Standing at the Edge. And I suspect that your willingness to come on my podcast has something to do with wanting to talk about that book. Now, I've seen an advance copy of it, and it's quite an impressive document, going into such issues as engagement and compassion and empathy in the most difficult situations — how to bring those qualities into war zones and famine relief and so on. And it's actually a manual, as far as I can tell. There's a lot of practice and a lot of really clear understanding of how to do it.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: But it's not a how-to book. I think it's a book that's edgier, if you will, than a how-to book.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And what's the name of the book?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It's called Standing at the Edge.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So it's edgier, and it's Standing at the Edge.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Right. Finding Freedom Where Fear and Courage Meet.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Great title. So what's your intention in publishing this book?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: You know, I've had the privilege of sitting with dying people over many decades, and working in the penitentiary system, having students who are clinicians, human rights activists, politicians, lawyers — and bearing witness to the suffering that they encounter when they are engaged in service to others. And I also know that experience myself, where my altruism has not always been balanced. And I began to look at some of the powerful human virtues that make for health in our society — including altruism, empathy, integrity, respect, and engagement — and have recognized that there are shadows to each of these. And those shadows cause suffering, not only for the individuals who are caught in the grip of pathological altruism, but it can harm those whom we're endeavoring to serve, or even the institutions that we're serving in, or the countries that we're trying to serve. Or empathic distress, where we're in too great a resonance physically, emotionally, cognitively with another — we're too fused, and we experience empathic distress and empathic overload. And integrity breaks down and we experience moral suffering. Or when respect is absent and disrespect is present. Or burnout, which is the shadow side of engagement.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: I wrote the book for a number of reasons, one of which is that we live in a really fraught time. There's extraordinary challenges and opportunities in our world today. And how do we use these positive and inherent qualities of the human character in a way that is skillful? How do we deploy them in a way that's skillful? And how do we be aware that when we fall over the edge from altruism into pathological altruism, that compassion is actually the lever, or the medium, of transformation of these shadow states? So that's the core thesis in the book.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: That compassion, which has not been so well understood in Western society, has — phenomenally enough — no downside. In spite of what many people feel, even the term "compassion fatigue" sounds like compassion can waste you. But what's happening in social psychology and neuroscience now is fascinating, in the sense that it is validating what contemplatives have long known: that compassion, like wisdom — these are two qualities that are interconnected — are fundamental to our human nature.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: This is the angle on the book that I think is so deep and unusual and fascinating. Instead of being a text that merely tells people to be compassionate and altruistic and respectful, you're showing how even individuals who have a very deep relationship with those qualities, or a deep commitment to bringing those qualities forward, can often fall into the shadow side of it. And that's very unusual, and I think a much needed thing to bring out.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It's edgy.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's edgy, yeah. It's like a beautiful text for people whose work in life is really about serving others. And what I saw going through the book is how you can make sure you're staying in the healthy expression of those virtues. So you're talking about compassion — what would you say is the shadow side of compassion?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: You know, my perspective is very simple in relation to compassion: that it doesn't have a shadow side. But it's often conflated with empathy. And it's not to say that empathy isn't essential, because clearly a world without empathy is a world where we are dead to each other. But it is also not uncommon that we tilt from healthy empathy into empathic distress, into over-identification with people — and not just people who are suffering. A really unusual example of this — Paul Bloom wrote about this in his book on empathy — is how in the Second World War an entire nation of Germans identified cognitively with Hitler, where they were kind of looking out through Hitler's eyes and adopted his view. And that's a kind of mind reading, or cognitive empathy. And the result is that there are behaviors that arise out of this attitude or view or way of seeing that were horrendously destructive. And so perspective taking, or mind reading, is important. It's important to be able to see how others see the world. It's really essential, it's fundamental. But when the experience of cognitive empathy swamps our own integrity, then we're faced — and others are faced — with serious consequences, like what happened in the Second World War in the Third Reich.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, you are, I think, contrasting empathy with compassion in the way that, for example, Tania Singer does, where empathy is feeling what another person feels, or cognitively sort of seeing their worldview like they see their worldview.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And then compassion is actually the motivation to help them — if I'm not mistaken, or please correct me.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Well, you know, when I began to look at compassion, I recognized that there were certain features characteristic of compassion, and they include attention — our capacity to be able to actually lend our attention to another. And having attentional balance allows us to perceive things with more clarity. And then prosociality: our capacity to feel concern, kindness, appreciation, gratitude — a whole range of prosocial states. One can't be antisocial and compassionate at the same time; in a way it's a sort of behavioral oxymoron.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: And then one's intention. It takes intentionality that is based in the aspiration to end suffering, which is, from the Buddhist perspective, the cultivation of bodhicitta: I vow to awaken in order to end the suffering of all beings. Which is grounded in this experience of moral character — being able to have moral sensitivity, to actually sense what is happening not only in our own subjectivity, but in the intersubjectivity of the whole realm of our knowing and experiencing. And then it takes moral nerve. In other words, the aspiration to end suffering takes moral nerve. It takes commitment, determination, strength, the courage to actually step into the mandala of suffering and to work it. Sometimes stepping into it means doing nothing. Sometimes it means doing something really big, or maybe something just very subtle — maybe it's just a touch of your hand to the hand of another. But it takes a kind of moral nerve. And this term, by the way, was a term that I picked out of a text from the author Joan Didion. I really love "moral nerve."

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It's a strong back, equanimity, determination. And compassion also involves insight — not only insight into our own subjectivity and capacities and where we're triggered, but insight into… again, this is out of the work of social psychology, of Daniel Batson, Tania Singer, Nancy Eisenberg — that if we don't distinguish self from other, we can become overwhelmed from our experience of empathy. So this is kind of contrary to the nondual perspective, which is your thing, of course. But from the point of view of social psychology, and how empathy can be healthy: from one point of view it's very important to distinguish self from other. Like when I was in Nepal, in the room where a little girl who was severely burned, her wounds were being debrided, and I had this deep identification with her, and she was suffering so much — and at a certain point I had to make that distinction: I am not her.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Otherwise, I was going to pass out to a dead faint right on the floor. And so that capacity to make that distinction is a kind of meta-awareness that allows us to both feel the suffering of another, but also at the same time to realize: I am not that other. And another aspect of insight that is very important — His Holiness the Dalai Lama always talks about this, saying, all beings want to be happy. Even a microorganism on a sugar gradient is looking for something nourishing. They don't want to run away from the sugar gradient, they're going up it. And even in working in the prison system with men who have murdered others — I worked on death row and in maximum security as a volunteer for six years, with really difficult, complicated human beings — whatever their crimes were, the terrible things they did to other people, rape and murder, they wanted to be happy too. And so, the insight into: all beings want to be happy. And then the final piece in this suite of elements — which are all trainable elements, Michael, which is really powerful.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Well, I want to mention one other thing, Michael. That is, compassion entails this capacity that we have to give our best, even when our best is only 20 percent. At that moment, we've given our best. But it also involves its complement: not being attached to outcome. Some people don't get that at all — "What are you talking about?" But it is: how do you give your best, and at the same time know you really can't control outcome? In fact, if you try to control it, often more harm arises.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Then the last feature that I identified, Michael, in this suite of features of compassion — and I look at compassion as a complex dynamical system; the emergent process of this suite of features that I've just outlined is compassion — this last feature is embodiment. Whether we're in a wheelchair, or like Stephen Hawking, where the body has dropped away, still we're in the body. And even though Hawking can barely move, I believe that he is thinking about, or operating from, the body of the whole world. So his insights, his kind of cosmic and political insights, relate to his bodhisattva's heart, which still beats, and it's about how do we end suffering. So embodiment is an important feature in compassion, because it involves as well not just our somatic experience — and not everybody is like Hawking, as an example; he's kind of like a brain that has very little body left — but his concern, not just about the farthest star, so to speak, but about our intimate human experience on this earth, is undeniable.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So how do we enact compassion in the world? If we have a situation of empathic distress, where we're overwhelmed with our empathy for another, how can we use compassion to counteract that situation?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: So in the outlining of these features of compassion, we begin really with attention, and to see how our attention is easily hijacked by ungrounded emotional reactivity to that which we're facing.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's really interesting. I often have the experience of feeling the distress of animals that I'm presented with — a bird or a dog or something — and just how, to me, they're people, just like anybody else, and they have such a beautiful presence. And then in connection with them, you see their suffering, and it's very intense. And yet that's just pure empathy. So I'm curious how one would — or I would — begin to change that. So you're saying the first step is to have just attention to that emotional uprising?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It's first noticing. And that's what we're trained to do in meditation, particularly when we're in the beginning phases of meditation. We notice when our thought stream, so to speak, has been hijacked to Chicago or Birmingham or New York, or the latest spat we've had with our good friend. So it's that capacity to notice.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: In the case of, for example, you're sitting with your dog — which is, for many of us, the most undefended relationship we've had. Here's this being. I might be on Facebook and I'll see a little video of a dog and I can just feel my whole heart melt. Just the same way when I see a picture of a baby. It's a very undefended relationship. And if you see a creature who's suffering, and then there's this identification with the creature, you're very upregulated and vulnerable, and you have taken on the suffering of the dog or the baby. And as a result of that, you experience secondary trauma — or vicarious trauma. You're being traumatized either by hearing about or witnessing the suffering of another.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: And so this is where attention becomes really important, because if we pay attention to what's happening — or lend our attention, rather, to what's happening in the body — and we start to notice the response of the body to witnessing suffering: suddenly our blood pressure drops, or it goes up, suddenly our gut tightens, our shoulders go up, we begin to have a kind of fight, flight, or freeze response, fear response, to the presence of suffering. And then our aspiration to be of service hopefully engages, and we invite ourselves to get grounded, to make the distinction between self and other, to remember that we're there to end suffering, not to add to the quotient of it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So feeling the other being's suffering isn't necessarily helping in any way?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Well, I think it does help, but feeling too much doesn't help, because we move into overwhelm. So, you know, Michael, one of the things I did after I was a distinguished visiting scholar at the Library of Congress, where I had a chance to do this heuristic map of compassion — what I wanted to do, because of working with so many people in the end-of-life care field, and also in relation to issues of justice and education and so forth, I felt like it would be useful to take this map and to develop an actual process that one could deploy or engage at the moment of encountering suffering, as a means to cultivate compassion. And so I developed this process called GRACE. And it's a mnemonic standing for: gathering your attention; recalling your intention;

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: attending, or attuning, to yourself — which includes your physical experience, your emotional experience, your cognitive experience — so you can get grounded and see your biases, the filters that are potentially distorting how you perceive the other; and then attuning to the other physically, emotionally, cognitively: body, heart, and mind. And from that perspective, then, the C of GRACE is considering what will really serve: looking deeply, using the information coming from your body, your heart, your mind, and what you've learned through allowing the experience of another to be included into yours. And from that, consider what will really serve. And then the E of GRACE is engage.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: When you have that insight into what will serve, we engage. And sometimes it's like a micro-moment, but sometimes engagement happens in a slower way. We'll say, "I need some time to really look at this with you and to see what is really going to serve here." And then the second part of the E of GRACE is to end. How do you bring into conclusion the experience of compassion? You might need to ask for forgiveness. You might need to express appreciation. You might need to summarize and reflect. So how do you end — interpersonally, or, if that's not appropriate, internally — a connection where compassion has been actualized?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So that final E is like a closing of the compassion event.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So have you been engaging this strategy specifically in your work recently yourself? I know you were just in Burma, I believe.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Actually, we were working — we brought the Nomads Clinic to refugee camps of Rohingya people in Kathmandu. So no, not in Burma, nor Bangladesh. Hundreds of men, women, and many children have gone north out of these camps, through Bangladesh, and made their way into Kathmandu. And there are these refugee camps where our clinic has served.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And let me just ask you, changing gears slightly about that experience — what would you like to say about what's going on there?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Well, Michael, I didn't realize that there were Rohingya refugees in Kathmandu. We go to Nepal every year with our Nomads Clinic and work with Nepali clinicians and Western clinicians, serving people in very remote areas of the Himalayas where there's no access to health care. And I've been doing it since 1980. And it's a great experience. We have a team of really exceptional Nepali doctors, nurses, physical therapists, acupuncturists, Tibetan healers, Tibetan doctors — this fantastic team of people, dentists, Nepali dentists, Dr. Prabhu Dorji — wonderful people.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Before we go out into the field, we take our Western clinicians with our Nepali clinicians. It's like after the earthquake in Nepal a few years ago: we went to a refugee camp, or a camp where people whose villages had been destroyed had resettled in Kathmandu for a couple of years, and we served in those camps as a kind of check-in with our clinicians. And so last year we went to these Rohingya refugee camps. I had been asked by one of our Nepali colleagues to help with medical services and other things. So we paid for surgeries and we supported clinics for people in the camps. But we hadn't gone until the end of August. Really, it was at the climax of the genocide in Myanmar. And it was truly shocking to listen to these people speak about what was happening in their villages, to look at their mobile phones with videos of their relatives being shot and burned. I mean, it's just overwhelming. So we have been in the process since that time of feeding everybody in those camps since August, and also providing health care, providing clothing and blankets and so on. But, as I said, my initial experience, Michael, was of overwhelm.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: You know, I'm watching this video being sort of held up to me as I'm in this hot tin shack in the middle of the camp with three men, one of whom had tears streaking down his cheeks, and the man in the center showing me this video of what was happening in his village. And I also realized, as this feeling of horror was rising inside of me, that, again, I was there to serve. So: getting grounded, remembering why I was there, and engaging GRACE at that moment.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: How did they respond to you as a Buddhist cleric in a situation where they're being persecuted by a nominally Buddhist government?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: So that's a great question, Michael. I felt part of the reason that, for me personally, it was important to go to those camps was to apologize. It was a personal apology. I can't apologize on behalf of Buddhism — I'm just one person, but I am a Buddhist. And this violence is being perpetrated by Buddhists. And so I had on my rakusu, I had on my robe, and the people in the camp, a number of them spoke to what they had been subjected to. And then I was asked to speak, and I expressed deep gratitude for them allowing me to come into the camp. The doctors on our team were there, and all of us shared the sense of profound shame and remorse and grief — that these Muslim people who had no place to go had actually fled from a Muslim country as well, Bangladesh, because they were subjected to abuse there, to Nepal, which is a very poor country, the poorest country after Afghanistan. But there's less discrimination there, more respect and inclusion.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: I just — I apologized. I felt ashamed. It's hard to grasp how, for me personally, how this ethnic cleansing could be carried out by Buddhists. But if we look at what happened in Cambodia, we have to take responsibility when, in the name of our religion, the acts of horror happen. And so, yeah. I was grateful that we have been able as Buddhists to do something. And Jabbar, one of the men in the camp, said, "You know, in Myanmar Buddhists are killing us. Here in Nepal Buddhists are healing us." I was very touched by what he said. And at the same time, this is just a small drop in a great ocean of suffering.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: A drop of goodness in a great ocean of suffering.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: I don't know how the aversion that people in Myanmar feel toward the Rohingya, how that will resolve. But I hope we can help in its resolution.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, you have been a scientist for more than 50 years, probably 55 years or more — a medical anthropologist. And it's fascinating to me how these days we're in a milieu of investigation: science investigating Buddhism, science investigating states of mind that are related to meditation. That's been, I would say, kind of a big deal for at least 10 years, you know, with Mind and Life, and various work of Richie Davidson and Judson Brewer, and really dedicated lab people doing their research. And of course, you've been involved in that with Tania Singer and everyone as well. On the other hand, you have this very unusual and fascinating background working with indigenous shamanic communities, who are presenting quite a different worldview than the scientific worldview. I'm curious — to me, one of the most powerful experiences, and really not just a powerful momentary experience but an ongoing, continuous presence for me, was a long retreat that I did in the forest, like three months. And after a while it was very clear that the forest and the turkeys and the various creatures there were doing all the work for me. They were the meditators, and all I had to do was just kind of be with that. And I just finished your book called The Fruitful Darkness, which is more focused in that way on the connection with the earth, the connection with silence and stillness. I'm curious how you see that fitting in, in any way, to this whole new wave of science, quote, "proving" our meditative experience — which of course I'm very interested in — you know, apps being used for meditation, this whole, in a way, speedy and intense connection with Buddhism and one's practice. How do you see the silence and stillness and the earth-focused experience fitting in with that?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: I'm remembering some words about science in relation to our own subjective experience from Francisco Varela. And Cisco felt that the most powerful lab was between our ears. I think science has been tremendously helpful in validating what practitioners have always known, and great teachers of the axial period clearly spoke about — the value of investigating our subjectivity, our direct experience. And with the increase of urbanization, and now the mind in a way extended through our digital devices, we seem to be further and further away from the natural world, many of us. In Japan, there's something called forest bathing — being in the natural world, where you're in the less speedy context of a greater, less constructed subjectivity than, say, San Francisco, where we are today. And somehow being in the forest — or, you know, now we're looking at the value of being next to the ocean — has positive effects on the nervous system. I mean, in the Pali Canon one of the prescriptions that the Buddha gave for practice is: find a quiet place in nature.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: And yet I was talking with a young friend in Hong Kong who said to me, "I've only lived in the concrete world." And he's excited — he's the brother of one of our clinicians in the Nomads Clinic, and he's going to join us in Dolpo in September. He said, "I've never been in the wilds." And he's really nervous and excited, because he knows that his nervous system will change. Or like a wonderful Japanese monk practitioner from Fukui who came to do a vision fast with me maybe 20 years ago. And I asked him about what his experience in the natural world was. And he said, "Well, I've been to three baseball games."

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Those are outside, I guess.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Yes, they are outside. So the challenge that we're facing at this time is the destruction of the natural world. And the natural world also seems to be rearing its head up from our consumption of goods, in terms of climate change, with hurricanes and desertification. And so we're in a kind of tipping point, as Bill McKibben calls it, where climate change is threatening civilization. At the same time, we're being asked to wake up and take responsibility, and to actually see if we can reverse the habits of mind that make forest bathing impossible — because we're cutting down all the forests, turning our beaches into collection systems for plastic. We're at a time where we have to, I feel, take full responsibility for the changes that we're incurring, and to think about what we're leaving for our children, but also how can we create the context where we value the natural world and can allow ourselves not to be threatened by it, or turn it into a commodity, but to go there to be healed.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And from your perspective as both a Buddhist teacher and a shamanic practitioner or healer, how can we do that most effectively? Most of us — let's say someone living here in San Francisco who wants to really begin to make that connection more explicit and meaningful in their life. Is it as simple as, you know, go sit on the beach, or…?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Maybe. Yeah. You know, walk up Mount Tam, follow the trails out to the headlands. But also I think that, because so many people have access to education, to become more aware of cause and effect — and to see what practice can do, what meditation practice can do: allow the mind to perceive things more clearly. So we understand cause and effect, and we begin to regulate our behaviors that are contributing to this dysphoric time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good. So what are you seeing currently that you would like to direct people's attention towards most poignantly?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Michael, I'm really excited about this book. I feel like the book Standing at the Edge doesn't invalidate the difficulties that we experience when we fall over the edge, but gives us a view that our character can be strengthened through catastrophe. And that it's not like a situation when, for example, we are suffering from empathic distress, we feel our world is collapsing internally and we feel aversion toward facing suffering — we actually look at that collapse and say, ah, this is a time for a deep exhale, letting go, taking care of. It's a kind of mindfulness bell.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: I think we're hearing a big mindfulness bell at this time. Not simply about taking a backward step, to quote Zen Master Dogen, but the value of stopping, the value of inquiry, of turning our attention not only into our own subjectivity, but creating the means for our own subjectivity to be radically inclusive — to include others, and to be able to actually modulate our experience of the experience of others in a way that we don't become sick, we don't become ungrounded, we don't experience collapse as a result of radical inclusion. And when we do, we use that time initiatically. We use that time as a way to look deeply and ask: what have I learned here? What has served? How can I serve a world that is so fragile, so vulnerable? How can I see where the points of resilience are, and begin to help to sort of build capacity in the world, instead of draw capacity from it?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Something I encounter quite often is practitioners of Buddhism or some meditation tradition who seem to have retreated from this edge of engagement that you're really promoting, into a kind of cocoon of nothing mattering — or, in my opinion, it seems almost nihilistic withdrawal. I'm curious what you would say to someone who was in that place.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: You know, there are many dharma doors. I would say that is one of them. Not everybody has the makeup to be so-called on the front lines, to engage in social transformation. And I also think that there are phases that we go through. There are times when we're actually too sensitive and unable to metabolize the shocks of society; that the exhale is really important. At times of deep internal practice, or of isolation, or hermiting — these are very generative. And if we don't take advantage of those times, sometimes they're given to us: for example, we become ill because of overexposure to psychosocial and physical toxins. So I don't find fault with anybody who is hermiting. I have to hermit myself. I have to take that exhale seriously. I have to go to the wilderness in order to allow myself to, you know, press sensitively the restart button. I don't have the internal elasticity to be able to sustain myself healthily in the landscape of suffering. I'm not that kind of enlightened person. I have to have the inhale moments, the moments of engagement, of taking the breath in and going out into the world. But I also have to have moments of deep letting go.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: And for some people it's not moments, it's not days — months, sometimes it's years. And I have to say, I respect the different capacities of different individuals. It's not to say everybody is going to be Wangari Maathai, planting a million trees; everybody is going to be Fannie Lou Hamer, working for SNCC and getting the voter registration happening in the South, 24/7. We all have different makeups, and we have to basically do what is appropriate within the range of our capacities. And part of what the book is about is that some of us require more of an exhale than others — and it's to learn when that is the case, to respect it. Otherwise, pathological altruism unfolds. We go over the edge.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So we live in a pretty exciting time right now. There's a lot of really intense things happening. I was noticing today that the Arctic is 60 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than it should be — six-zero degrees warmer — and all the political chaos and so on. This weekend — I live in West Oakland — three people were shot on my block, just randomly. There's a lot to feel overwhelmed about. But I'm curious: what do you feel hopeful about, or inspired by, currently?

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: Well, I feel hopeful about your equanimity when you talk about 60 degrees warmer than it should be, or three people on your block were shot. It's not that you're saying this in a dissociated way, but you're noticing. You choose to not put your head in the sand, but to notice the suffering. And you're doing what is appropriate for you about bringing hope into the world. Rebecca Solnit's book Hope in the Dark — and she's written another one, A Paradise Built in Hell. There are so many examples of people, of communities, of groups, of nations — like Bhutan is a good example — really espousing an ethos of happiness. I feel that the toxic aspects of our society are in fact the minority, even though they're the loudest; that there is so much goodness in the current landscape, and that in a certain way our media is colonizing us with hopelessness. And yet I feel not colonized by hopelessness. I feel inspired by the many people I meet every single day who are operating from a base of deep integrity.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Roshi, thank you so much for coming on the program.

transcript.speaker: Joan Halifax
transcript.text: It has been my pleasure. Wonderful to see you again, Michael.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So good to see you again as well. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's it for this episode of Deconstructing Yourself.

glossary.definition: Japanese honorific for a senior Zen teacher, literally "old teacher"; a title conferred on someone authorized to teach.
A school of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in China (Chan) and Japan, emphasizing seated meditation (zazen) and direct insight over doctrinal study.
Sanskrit, "awakening mind/heart": the aspiration to attain awakening for the sake of ending the suffering of all beings; the core motivation of the Mahayana path.
A being who vows to attain awakening in order to liberate all beings, postponing personal liberation for the sake of others.
A small rectangular garment worn around the neck in Zen, a miniature version of the monastic robe (kesa), received at lay or priestly ordination.
Eihei Dogen (1200–1253), founder of the Soto school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shobogenzo; the source of the phrase "take the backward step."
The earliest complete collection of Buddhist scriptures, preserved in the Pali language, the scriptural basis of Theravada Buddhism.
A traditional expression for the many valid gateways or approaches to practice and awakening; different temperaments require different paths.
A circular symbolic diagram of a sacred realm in Indian and Tibetan traditions; used here figuratively for the whole field or territory of suffering one enters.
Sanskrit, "skillful means": adapting the teaching to the needs and capacity of the listener. Also the name of Joan Halifax's Zen center in Santa Fe.
Sanskrit, "wisdom": the discerning insight into the nature of reality, especially emptiness; paired with compassion (karuna) as the two wings of the path.
A modern movement, associated with Thich Nhat Hanh and others, applying Buddhist practice directly to social, political, and ecological suffering.

A five-step protocol developed by Joan Halifax for cultivating compassion in the moment of encountering suffering: Gather attention, Recall intention, Attune to self and other, Consider what will serve, Engage and End.
The over-identification with another's suffering to the point of personal overwhelm; distinguished from compassion, which remains grounded and oriented toward helping.
Helping behavior that, through imbalance or lack of boundaries, harms the helper, the person helped, or the institution served.
A Muslim ethnic minority of Rakhine State in Myanmar, subjected to mass violence and forced displacement, especially in 2017.
A remote high-altitude region of northwestern Nepal with a Tibetan Buddhist culture, visited by Halifax's Nomads Clinic.
Shinrin-yoku, a Japanese practice of unhurried immersion in a forest environment for the sake of physical and psychological health.
